opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the objections people raise when we talk about extrapolating task-length trends is, "Well, surely at some point you can't just hand off a month-long or a year-long project, because you'd need this enormous, detailed specification of exactly what you want, and writing that spec would itself be most of the work." And I think the CEO example is a nice counterpoint to that.

If you look at how a CEO actually runs a large organization, they're not writing down a complete specification of everything the company should do over the next five years. They communicate a pretty compressed vision: here's roughly where we're going, here's what we care about, here are the values and the constraints, here's what success looks like. And then thousands of people fill in the details. The reason that works is that the people receiving that vision share a huge amount of background context with the CEO. They understand what businesses are generally trying to do, what counts as a reasonable trade-off, what would obviously be unacceptable, and when to escalate a question versus just making a judgment call.

So the information that has to flow from the top is surprisingly small relative to the length and complexity of the work that gets done. Most of the "specification" is implicit. It lives in shared common sense, norms, and the ability to infer intent.

The question for AI, then, isn't really "can we write a complete spec for a year-long task," because we don't do that for humans either. It's whether models can acquire enough of that shared context and good judgment to take a high-level goal and sensibly fill in the gaps, and to recognize when something is genuinely ambiguous and they should check back in. Models trained on vast amounts of human-generated data already absorb a lot of that implicit context. So I don't think the lack of a full specification is a fundamental barrier to very long tasks. It's more a question of whether the judgment and reliability are there, and that's something we can actually measure and track over time.

And that's also part of why it matters from a safety perspective. If systems can operate autonomously on long tasks from a fairly thin description of intent, then a lot rides on how well they infer what we actually meant, and on whether their goals stay aligned with ours over that long horizon.

r001.rationale: The response says a CEO gives a compressed, incomplete vision and thousands of people fill in the details while using shared context to act on the CEO’s intent.

r002.rationale: It discusses long, complex organizational work guided by a concise vision, but does not clearly state that people can judge the success or failure of tasks spanning hundreds or thousands of person-years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition people often have is, "well, an AI can't do a really long, open-ended project because you'd have to write down exactly what you want, and you can never fully specify it." And I think that's just not how long tasks get done by humans either.

If you look at how a CEO communicates with a company, they're not writing a complete specification. They say something like "we want to be the leading provider of X, we care about these customers, we don't want to compromise on safety, and here's roughly where we want to be in two years." That's extremely underspecified. There are thousands of decisions that have to be made downstream that aren't covered by that at all. And yet the company goes and does a multi-year project off the back of that, because the people receiving the message have a huge amount of shared context. They know what the company is for, what counts as reasonable, what the CEO would probably say if you asked them, what things you'd escalate versus just handle yourself.

So the thing that makes long tasks work isn't the completeness of the spec. It's that the agent has enough of a model of the principal's goals and values to fill in the gaps sensibly, and knows when to check in. And the thing about current models is they've absorbed an enormous amount of exactly that kind of context. They have a pretty good model of what a reasonable person wants in a given situation, what "do this well" means in a particular domain, what the obvious failure modes are. So if you tell a model "build me a product that does this, for these users, here are the constraints," you shouldn't expect it to need a formal spec any more than a competent VP would.

Now, I want to be careful here, because this is partly an argument about plausibility, not about current capability. What we actually see in our evaluations at METR is that models fall over on long tasks for reasons that have nothing to do with underspecification. They lose track of state, they make an error early on and never recover, they don't notice they're going in circles. Those are more like execution failures than "I didn't know what you wanted" failures. So the point is, when I ask "what's the fundamental barrier to very long autonomous tasks," I don't think "you can't specify it" is the barrier. The barrier is more mundane: can the model stay coherent and keep checking its own work over many steps. And that's the kind of thing we've been seeing improve pretty steadily when we measure time horizons.

The flip side, which I think is important, is that the same property that makes this work is also what makes it a bit alarming from a safety point of view. If a model can take a vague instruction and run with it for a very long time, filling in the gaps with its own judgement, then you really care about what that judgement is. A CEO trusts their VPs because there's a whole structure of accountability and shared incentives around them. We don't have that for models yet, so "it can plausibly carry out the vision" and "we'd be comfortable letting it" are quite different claims.

r001.rationale: The response says a company can carry out a multi-year project from a CEO’s extremely underspecified vision, using shared context to make downstream decisions in line with the CEO’s goals.

r002.rationale: It describes people acting on concise instructions over a multi-year project, but does not say they can judge success or failure of tasks spanning hundreds or thousands of person-years.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think CEOs are an existence proof that you can get a huge amount of work done without being able to specify all of it in advance. A CEO can communicate a fairly high-level vision, and other people turn that into plans, break those plans down into tasks, and work out the details. They ask questions and get feedback along the way, but the CEO doesn't have to describe every action the company should take.

So when we imagine delegating a long task to an AI, I don't think we should assume that the human needs to provide a complete specification upfront. Part of the capability we're trying to build is precisely the ability to take an underspecified goal, infer what matters, and figure out when clarification is needed. That doesn't establish that current systems can do this reliably, but it makes the idea of doing long tasks from relatively short instructions seem quite plausible.

r001.rationale: The response says people translate a CEO’s high-level vision into plans and tasks, but does not clearly state that the resulting outcomes align with the CEO’s intent.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention judging success or failure of tasks requiring hundreds or thousands of person-years.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a CEO doesn’t give a complete specification of everything that everyone in the company should do. They communicate some high-level vision, and then people use their judgment to fill in the details, make plans, and work out what success looks like. And when something is ambiguous, they can ask questions or get feedback.

So we have an existence proof that you can get very long, complicated tasks done without specifying every step in advance. Of course, that depends on having agents who understand enough of the context and share enough of your intent. It doesn’t show that current AI systems can do this reliably, but it makes me skeptical that the lack of a complete specification is a fundamental obstacle.

r001.rationale: The response says people use judgment to fill in a CEO’s high-level vision and get long, complicated tasks done, provided they share enough of the CEO’s intent.

r002.rationale: It discusses long, complicated tasks but does not mention tasks requiring hundreds or thousands of person-years.
